Very, very thematic game. The setting is cool and the UI is absolutely top notch. Super immersive, and the writing is pretty good. The devs are super responsive and seem dedicated which is nice with indie games.

This is definitely a story based RPG but I can't see myself replaying it much like I would a more open ended hacking game like Uplink. I know there's content I missed, but it's pretty onerous to get to it.

[b]Why a negative review?[/b] The actual gameplay itself is pretty bland, when you boil it down. A far cry from Netrunner in that regard. You can crudely smash through a system to learn it, then "rollback" (aka restart) and play properly with your new meta knowledge. Most of the programs aren't balanced well against each other, and unless you're doing a specific run or attempting a certain build there's no reason to deviate or choose other approaches. Trace is your only real opposition, and if you can get around it (with a program like Mask) the levels are super boring as you slowly go through the motions, 2 commands at a time (followed by typing "end" each time). No hard/meaningful decisions, sacrifices, or anything that typically makes for compelling gameplay. Plus the animations are so slow when you have your next ~10-15 moves planned out and are just waiting for the game to let you do them.

And at the end of of the day I play games for the gameplay. You might be different, and so you might like it as a concise 7-9 hour story game. I certainly WANTED to like it, and am a bit sad to give it a negative. But as nice as the game looks, as cool as the devs seem, and as rare as unique hacking games are, I just can't recommend it.

review_text_raw:
Midnight Protocol is rich in ambience, in intrigue, in tangled relationships of regret and camaraderie confidently conveyed in nothing more than text, and in more than its fair share of ingenuity.

It's also, unfortunately, like playing chess with only five pieces against a kid who can, at any time, go "yeah no but I had this super power set up HERE, right, all along I had this set up I did, and that means you can't get my guy and, uh, and, um, and and and WHOOOAAA EARTHQUAKE FLIPPED THE BOOOOARD"

You, master hacker that you are, are allowed to do two - count 'em - two succulent and juicy things per turn, and have to sulkily type out 'end' to end your turn thereafter. The goal is to make the most of limited resources against a seemingly unassailable adversary through deft moves and cunning. So far, so hacking-mentality - applaudable.

Yet the execution just doesn't quite make it. Effective red-teaming is about having recon good to go in advance against your target, which you never have in Midnight Protocol - and which costs you precious scant actions per turn to execute in the field instead. The jaws close on you all the while, unless you turn off the Trace mechanic altogether in the game options, and then you're just left with slowly hopping two-by-two across the board poking at things and slowly slurping up cash.

The plot is compelling, rich in injustices and laced with what-ifs, and I wanted to push through and see more of it. Unfortunately, there's a fair bit of padding in the early game that killed the momentum for me. I get it's good to establish characters, lay down rules and playstyles etc., but it'd be so much more exciting for these tidbits to come through organically while enjoying unravelling the story.

A shame, as there's a lot of cool-factor to the whole affair - it just isn't that fun to play.

review_text_raw:
Midnight Protocol is an all right game that feels like it's one step away from worth recommending in every department.

Mechanically, using only keyboard commands winds up being more of a hindrance than an asset. So much targeting and movement could be done easier and quicker if the player was just allowed to click. Everything is already set up into a nice modern-looking GUI with discrete locations to mouse over and select. You just can't do that, and have to type anyway. 

As for the puzzles and difficulty, there are a few interesting challenges over the course of the game, but for the most part you are handled powerful enough tools that you rarely have to think very hard. There's also a lot of downtime while enemy turns and animations slowly play out, which means that even if you know the next ten moves you'll want to make, actually executing them can be tedious.

Plot-wise, the game sets up a specific narrative and conflict you will eventually become embroiled in and resolve, but it's a little light on motivations for the player to actually get invested. The story feels like it mostly depends on a couple big surprise twists to do the legwork, but without grounding the player before and after them, it doesn't feel like enough to make a great story.

Maybe if there was an absolute banger OST, or the solutions to the puzzles could get really really crazy, that would be enough to push the game over the cusp of greatness. As presented though, it feels overall a bit underwhelming.

review_text_raw:
First of all, the decision to shoehorn a keyboard-only interface was disastrously misguided. They took a game that was basically designed for a GUI and replaced the GUI with an awkward CLI. 

You know what's faster than typing in "map", just to look up the names of relevant nodes (the names of non-adjacent nodes being of course hidden from view for some reason and it's not like they are organized in a logical grid either), and then typing "sniper [node1] [node2]"? A SINGLE CLICK. Having to constantly reassign slices in order to optimize is another major pain. Almost every action could be done faster with a mouse and you feel it with everything you do.

This is of course the exact opposite of why hackers use the terminal. They use it because it's faster and more powerful (or they have no other choice for interacting with a remote host). They don't use it in order to deliberately make things slower and dumber for themselves.

I guess if you don't have this in mind when you play the game, you might feel like a 1337 haxxor pwning distant networks with nothing but your keyboard. But if you do understand all of the above, you will likely feel like your time is being wasted with terrible UX design. 

If the puzzles weren't lame and/or the story was not a forgettable cyberpunk cliche, then maybe dealing with these UX issues would be worth it, but neither of that is true.

review_text_raw:
The game is a novel concept, but I have to unfortunately call a spade a spade here.

This game is a turn-based hacking game with RNG elements that make the game severely unfun. They also got some very clear inspiration from Hacknet with the main characters name being literally taken from the character from Hacknet, Data. There's also Clover, another homage to Hacknet (I believe). They even have a port command, except instead of PortHack it's PortSeek/PortSeeker.

Unfortunately I simply can't recommend this game. The fact that it's turn-based is fine, but the RNG element really just throws it under the water. If you want a hacking game, get Hacknet.

review_text_raw:
Midnight Protocol is a desktop/hacking sim, and like all of these games, has nothing to do with actual hacking and is utterly unrealistic.  So this is just a strategy (turn based or realtime, you choose) game where you plug away controlling nodes or whatever.  The game does work but it's needlessly convoluted.  I guess to illustrate this, it takes 1/10th the time to learn how to play an RTS like Command & Conquer for 10x the rewarding gameplay.  And even though it's only a 2D game, C&C also has better graphics than this. 

The game design is somewhat flawed in some ways, with a reliance on procgen and RNG that can make or break each challenge. But mostly the game falls flat hard on a very weak and amateurish technical and visual presentation, and sloppy, and in some ways offensive interface design. 

On the upside, the game does feature customisable controls and resolution, so at least some of the basic, minimum requirements have been met.  Unfortunately there's a number of other technical defects and shortcomings which contribute to the game being difficult to recommend to gamers.

The game features lazy minimalist/untextured low-polygon "retro" assets and visuals, making this look like a barely functional 3D game from the early 1990s.  The lack of textures is a method that lazy devs often use to disguise their lack of talent/interest in doing the graphics properly and trying to disguise it under the name of "art", or "We made it look bad on purpose", which really isn't something gamers should have to put up with.  It's unclear why the developers weren't willing to arrange high quality, high polygon count contemporary assets and high resolution textures for the game.  It looks bad as a result of their decisions, and that's just another reason to avoid it.

To make matters worse, there's no mouse input, despite this being sold on PC as if it were a PC game.  This is unacceptable and somewhat insulting.  I know this is on purpose to make it seem like some kind of cool "hacker" game but this is annoying. Don't do this.  No developer should ever dictate to gamers how a game is to be played, ever. 

These technical defects push this game below acceptable standards for any modern PC game.

Midnight Protocol didn't appeal much to the people who own a copy of the game, either.  It has achievements, and they show us a very clear picture that the game didn't really capture any interest from gamers.  The most commonly and easily attained achievement is for finishing the tutorial, trivial to get, but less than 39 percent of players bothered to get that far before uninstalling the game.  Hardly a success story, gamers just weren't all that interested in the game.

So, should you buy this game?  Is this one of the best of the 100,000+ games on Steam?

Midnight Protocol has the laughable, eye-watering price of $15 USD, for which you could easily get any number of older AAA games.  Given the defects and quality issues with the game, coupled with the unrealistic price, this is impossible to recommend.

For comparison, the $15 asking price for this game could get you games like "Mass Effect Andromeda", "Project Zomboid" or "Stellaris".  Quality, professionally made games like those are frequently on sale cheaper than this.

Cannot really say recommend or not - to me it is a 5/10 game. Overall, it is not quite like a hacking game but more like a chess game. So if you like it - good worth a try. If you are expecting something similar to other hacking games or richer experience - not really your choice.

Good part: UI and music are good. Story line of the first half goes really well with many side stories to enrich the characters. [spoiler] Like the idea of angel vs evil choices.[/spoiler] 

Bad part: After [spoiler]introducing the ices and trackers[/spoiler], the game starts to get boring although the difficulty level is increasing - it starts to be the same core [spoiler]playing with just more ices, more tracking techniques, less time/steps[/spoiler]. Story is good before [spoiler]signal reports you to Snail and Clover - and then the story goes quickly with your choice with much confusion. [/spoiler] For multi-language players, there is a bug that the information downloaded from data nodes shrink to a level that you cannot read. It is annoying so I finally played with English in the end.

Let's start with the positives. The visuals are very good, very "hackery" and just very pleasing to look at. It's also keyboard only, which further enhances the immersion.

And this is about it when it comes to the positives.

It's almost fundamentally not a hacking game. You could easily swap out all of the "commands" for just fantasy spells. You're not breaking into systems to gather information, to gather passwords to use on other networks (i.e. puzzle solving). Each "mission" is fundamentally independent. You're there to get money (or complete objectives for the story) and then leave.

There's also the weird RNG aspect of the game. Your "attacks" against "firewalls" can "crit". Not to mention, how many actions waste your action points, which is also complemented by how few turns you actually from being caught.

The developer has a solid foundation to creating an interesting hacking game. But if they're going to do a RNG/RPG turn-based game, then stick to fantasy/sci-fi instead.

Not to mention, how many actions waste your action points, which is also complemented by how few turns you actually from being caught. The developer has a solid foundation to creating an interesting hacking game. But if they're going to do a RNG/RPG turn-based game, then stick to fantasy/sci-fi instead.

[url=https://steamcommunity.com/id/beatnuki/recommended/1162700/]I pretty much gotta agree with this review[/url].

The developers advertised it on Netrunner adjacent boards. Unfortunately, that's as far as the Netrunner elements go.

You're playing a computer hacker (aka: "Runner" which isn't the term here, so not Netrunner releated) breaking into systems to figure out what has gone on since you were released from jail. Mayhem and hacking ensues.

But the thing is: For all the talk about being Netrunner inspired... it doesn't work. Both you and the AI/SysOp have two actions a turn (compared to Netrunners' 4 Runner 3 SysOp actions a turn). This would be fine... [b][i]IF[/i] the gameplay wasn't timed with the "trace" mechanic[/b] (unlike Netrunners, you can't remove it and you can't buy over the SysOp/Corp to bounce it/avoid the trace).

So you're racing against the clock, facecheck (slam into an ICE defense) and... get fucked over massively in terms of the timer/trace raising in addition to losing an action to where you can't course correct same turn. This means you'll get "trace++" 2+ traces in addition to the end turn trace (which if some ICE is hit, turns off your "cloak" function to try to prevent/stop the trace from increasing, say HELLO to 2-3+ traces off a faceslam).

[i]This is where the game becomes unfun[/i] and if I didn't run into the above review, I would've quit instead of finding the "turn the trace mechanic off" and as the review states: That makes the game somewhat boring because you're [i]turning off an anxiety/timer mechanic[/i] but after a certain point you're like "ok, I'm screwed five ways, why have a sixth?"

Interesting story to go through, but honestly: No, not worth the money. Check the demo out, if you're able to put up with the bad design (needed some more passes to be a bit more fair on the players), go for it. But honestly? I can't recommend it.

Hopefully NetSpectre gives me the Netrunner-a-like I want, but I'm kind of doubting it.

Slay the Spire is pretty much the only one that comes close and even THAT isn't going for Netrunner, but took elements from it.

...My search continues...

review_text_raw:
Incredibly boring. Supposed to be 2060 or something,but you have screen shaking and flickering like you're using a 1980s monitor (luckily, this can be switched off). 90% of the interface is ugly greyscale. Plays a bit like Uplink in that you are "connected" to the computers in the game world, except mouse is disabled. Keyboard only. But your default screen is a GUI, so instead of clicking icons you hit the corresponding keys.
Hacking isn't much better, you move from node to node, run any programs you have equipped (max five for some reason) while taking turns between you and the trace program. Trace increases and when it hits max, bad things happen to you. Turn based means the typing commands makes zero sense, because your (in)ability to type quickly and correctly has zero impact on the game.
Seems there's a story there, but I'm not sticking around to find out. Refunded.
